newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria rejects allegations of tax evasion.
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria rejects allegations of tax evasion.

text.p: Bank Austria, the country's top bank, on Wednesday denied accusations of tax evasion connected to a 1994 dividend payment by clearing bank Kontrollbank (OeKB) to its main shareholders.

Far-right leader Joerg Haider on Tuesday claimed OeKB board member Gerhard Praschak's suicide at the weekend had been linked to a tax evasion scandal involving a secret payout of 140 million schillings ($12 million).

"The allegation that tax-evasion has been committed in connection with a dividend payment by OeKB to its shareholders, among them Bank Austria, is rejected in the strongest possible terms," the bank said in a statement.

Haider claimed that documents apparently mailed by Praschak to opposition parties and state prosecutors before his suicide contained clear evidence of such "secret" payments. Copies of the documents have been made available to reporters.

One page of the documents shows handwriting, said to be Praschak's, in which details of the payments are outlined. According to the notes, Bank Austria and Creditanstalt, the two key shareholders of OeKB, had pressed for a secret payment to avoid capital gains taxes.
Haider said the papers showed the payment was disguised as fees and provisions on credit lines opened to OeKB by the banks. The lines were never drawn upon.
Bank Austria said all payments to or from OeKB had been properly documented and that no secret dealings had taken place.

"The notes from the year 1994 refer to preliminary discussions by employees of OeKB and two of its shareholders. Because it became clear after an in-depth examination that these plans for various reasons were not viable, they were never realised," the bank said.
Experts said the payment details outlined in Praschak's notes would, if they had been turned into reality, amount to a clear breach of Austrian tax laws.
If it had taken place, "it would have been a clear case of tax evasion," said Roman Leitner of accountancy firm Leitner and Leitner.
